tldr: This paper presents GAUGE, a benchmark that comprehensively validates the physical fidelity of physics simulation engines and generative video world models against high-precision real-world measurements and physical parameters. The results reveal that even when visuals appear realistic, systems deviate substantially from physical laws in impulsive contact, rapid textile deformation, and gravitational acceleration scale.
hero_caption: Overview of the measurement-grounded benchmark GAUGE. High-precision trajectories and physical parameters obtained from real-world experiments across rigid bodies, textiles, and deformable objects serve as a common ground truth to uniformly diagnose both numerical physics simulators (left) and generative video world models (right).
overview:
In robot learning and policy evaluation, Sim2Real transfer—moving knowledge from simulators to the real world—has become the standard approach. Recently, generative video world models that directly predict future states as video have also attracted major interest as implicit simulators. However, there is a major pitfall: no matter how realistic things look on screen, the underlying physical dynamics are not necessarily correct. Existing evaluations often rely on human perception or visual similarity, failing to quantitatively diagnose which physical principles break down and how.

To address this, the authors developed GAUGE, an integrated benchmark that diagnoses the physical fidelity of both simulators and world models on a shared foundation of rigorous real-world physical measurements. They designed 22 physical task families covering rigid bodies, cables, textiles, and 3D volumetric deformable objects, collecting roughly 1,560 trajectory trials using millimeter-precision motion capture. Furthermore, dedicated instruments were used to physically measure friction coefficients, coefficients of restitution, textile tensile and bending stiffness, and deformable Young's moduli, which are attached as metadata.

Using this setup, the authors thoroughly evaluated three representative physics engines—Isaac Sim, Genesis, and Newton—along with six recent video generation models, including Cosmos3 and Wan. The results show that no physics engine is universally faithful across all tasks, with major discrepancies arising in impulsive collisions and rapid textile motions. Video world models, meanwhile, revealed a serious issue: even when generating visually clean parabolas or periodic motions, their internal accelerations and oscillation periods diverged completely from the real world, showing the right mathematical form but bogus physical parameters.
contributions: Built a high-precision motion-capture dataset of approximately 1,560 trials across 22 task families spanning rigid bodies, 1D cables, 2D textiles, and 3D deformable bodies.

Directly measured and identified physical parameters across diverse physical domains—including friction, restitution, textile constitutive laws, and volumetric moduli—using specialized instruments to provide them uniformly.

Established an evaluation pipeline that diagnoses numerical physics engines and generative video world models by separating the structure of governing equations from the accuracy of estimated parameters.

sections.heading: A diagnostic physics benchmark that looks beyond visual realism
sections.summary: In robotics policy learning, the physical fidelity of simulators and video world models is vital. However, visual appeal and physical dynamical accuracy are two different things, and existing metrics fail to diagnose which physical principles fail. GAUGE introduces an integrated benchmark grounded in real-world measurements and calibrated physical parameters.
sections.details:
In recent years, training pipelines that generate massive amounts of data in simulation environments to deploy robots in the real world have become widespread. Recent work, such as SIMPLER, has demonstrated that carefully matched simulations can predict real-world robot performance with considerable accuracy.

However, the success of this approach hinges entirely on how faithfully the underlying physics engines and predictive video world models reproduce real-world physics. A major obstacle here is that high visual fidelity does not guarantee physical fidelity. Even if a video or simulation looks smooth and true to life, incorrect contact forces, friction, or deformation dynamics will cause a robot to learn unnatural behaviors that exploit those simulation-specific artifacts.

Conventional benchmarks often rely on perceptual plausibility or human subjective ratings. Such approaches cannot separate how physics engines diverge from reality, nor can they tell whether a world model understands physical laws at the equation level or is merely mimicking plausible-looking texture changes.

Motivated by this, the authors built GAUGE, comprising 22 experimental task families spanning rigid bodies to deformable objects. By pairing millimeter-level real-world trajectories with experimentally measured physical parameters, GAUGE provides a common ground to diagnose both numerical physics engines and generative world models.

sections.heading: Unifying fragmented physics validation efforts into one benchmark
sections.summary: Prior studies have evaluated physics engines against physical hardware or assessed the physical consistency of world models, but they focused on isolated object types like rigid bodies or cloth. They also often relied on fitting parameters from trajectories rather than measuring them directly. GAUGE serves as the first standardized benchmark crossing these domains.
sections.details:
Related work broadly divides into three lines of research.

First is the real-world validation of physics engines. Past studies individually focused on rigid-body collisions and manipulation, or conversely specialized in cloth and deformable objects (such as PokeFlex and RGBench). However, these were confined to specific object categories and used fragmented score definitions. Furthermore, instead of directly measuring the physical parameters used in simulation, they frequently calibrated them by back-calculating from the very trajectories used for evaluation, limiting their ability to test true predictive capability.

Second is the physical consistency of generative video world models. Prior studies such as VideoPhy-2 mostly rely on subjective common-sense checks by humans or vision-language models (VLMs), without quantitatively tracking trajectory errors. While quantitative benchmarks like Physics-IQ and RIGIDBENCH have emerged, their evaluated physical laws are often restricted to simple scenarios like free fall, or their reference baseline is another simulator rather than the real world.

Third is the annotation of physical parameters. While datasets pairing videos with governing equations exist (such as IRIS), their friction and restitution damping values are merely apparent values back-calculated from trajectories, rather than parameters directly measured with material testing hardware.

GAUGE sets itself apart by measuring rigid-body contact, textile constitutive laws, and 3D continuum mechanics parameters with dedicated material testing instruments, providing them alongside real-world trajectories.

sections.heading: 22 tasks and two evaluation pipelines: the design philosophy of GAUGE
sections.summary: GAUGE comprises 22 tasks—8 rigid-body, 1 rope, 6 textile, and 7 deformable—spanning diverse material variations. It evaluates simulators using generalized trajectories that integrate geometric features, while evaluating world models with dedicated metrics separating equation structure from parameter accuracy.
sections.details:
3.1 Dataset Design and Collection Pipeline
The benchmark is designed to thoroughly probe fundamental physical phenomena rather than simple robot tasks. The 8 rigid-body tasks include slope sliding, collisions, Newton's cradle, and pendulums, while the 14 deformable tasks cover textile pulling, bending, and flinging, alongside sponge and rubber compression and twisting. Materials include wood, metal, and plastic, as well as 6 distinct woven fabrics and rubbers and urethane foams of varying hardness. Physical properties were rigorously measured beforehand using an inclined track, an air-bearing collision track, a Style3D fabric testing system, a tensile testing machine, and digital image correlation (DIC, which measures strain from surface pattern deformation).

3.2 Physics Engine Evaluation Pipeline
Three engines are tested: Isaac Sim (PhysX), Genesis, and Newton (MuJoCo). When initializing each task, no manual tuning is performed; measured material parameters are plugged directly into default configurations. To evaluate disparate systems, the authors define a "Generalized Trajectory" tracking 3D positions for rigid bodies, discrete Gaussian curvature at mesh vertices for textiles, and mesh triangle surface areas for 3D deformable objects. These are compared to real-world mean trajectories using frame-matched root mean squared error (RMSE) and dynamic time warping (DTW) to allow for temporal scaling.

3.3 World Model Evaluation Pipeline
Six models—Cosmos3 (Nano/Super), Wan (2.2/2.7), Seedance 2.0, and Genie 3—are evaluated across rigid-body tasks. Given an initial frame and a text prompt, models generate future videos, and Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3) segments the target object to extract 2D trajectories. In addition to a dynamics error (DE) checking consistency with equations of motion, the evaluation introduces the coefficient of determination ($R^2$) to test fit to expected equations and quadratic form improvement (QFI) to penalize spurious curvature, cleanly separating whether the equation form is correct from whether parameter values like acceleration are accurate.

captions.F2: The "generalized trajectory" representations used for physics engine evaluation: (a) 3D positions P for rigid bodies, (b) discrete Gaussian curvature K at each textile mesh marker, and (c) triangular element surface areas A on 3D deformable surface meshes, tracked over time to compare diverse objects under a unified framework.

sections.heading: A millimeter-precision real-world studio and unified inference setup
sections.summary: Real-world data was acquired using a 180 Hz optical motion capture system equipped with 16 infrared cameras. Physics simulators were executed on an RTX 4090 workstation, while world models performed inference with standardized image resolutions, aspect ratios, and unified text prompts.
sections.details:
4.1 Data Collection Environment
Experiments were conducted in a dedicated 2m x 2m x 2m studio surrounded by 16 NOKOV Mars9H infrared cameras mounted at three height levels. Operating at 180 Hz, the system provides sub-millimeter 3D positional precision. For rigid bodies, 6 mm diameter retro-reflective markers weighing approximately 0.5 g were attached to estimate 6-DoF poses. For textiles and deformable bodies, reflective sticker markers were applied in a grid on surfaces to construct local skeleton meshes. Marker masses are small enough to have negligible impact on object motion. Twenty independent real-world trials were recorded for each task to establish mean trajectories and uncertainty bands.

4.2 Physics Engine Execution Setup
Evaluations ran on a Windows workstation equipped with a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU. The simulation time step was set to 180 Hz for rigid bodies and textiles to match motion capture, and increased to 900 Hz for 3D deformable bodies to prevent numerical divergence. All recorded data were downsampled to 30 Hz for direct comparison with real-world trajectories.

4.3 World Model Inference Setup
Input images were padded to 832x480 pixels preserving aspect ratios (except for Genie 3, which requires a larger 1300x750 resolution). The Cosmos3 series and Wan-2.2 were run locally on RTX 4090 GPUs in a distributed environment, while commercial and closed models (Wan-2.7, Seedance 2.0, Genie 3) were generated via official APIs or web interfaces. Ablations testing the presence of negative prompts to suppress physically impossible behavior were also performed with standardized text.

captions.F3: Experimental studio setup and motion-capture tracking: (a) optical breadboard environment surrounded by 16 infrared cameras, (b) 6-DoF rigid-body pose estimation, (c) textile surface marker mesh tracking, and (d) 3D deformation tracking of urethane foam.

sections.heading: Impulsive contact, high-speed deformation, and scale errors: the findings
sections.summary: Physics engines exhibit distinct strengths and weaknesses, with errors surging during impulsive collisions, rapid textile motion, and 3D volumetric deformation. Video world models generated clean periodic and parabolic motions, but their gravitational accelerations and periods deviated from real-world values by more than a factor of two.
sections.details:
5.1 Physics Engine Results: No Universal Engine
In steady rigid-body contact and rotational motion (such as the turntable task), Isaac Sim achieved excellent results, yielding a normalized RMSE of 0.17—lower than the variance across real-world trials. Genesis performed strongly on the inclined slider (normalized RMSE of 0.58). However, when collisions occurred, performance deteriorated sharply. In the bouncing ball task, even the best engine recorded an RMSE over 15 times the baseline. In Newton's cradle, Isaac Sim and Newton achieved momentum transfer efficiencies (MTE) of only 0.20 to 0.26, while Genesis failed to complete the simulation reliably.

Discrepancies among solvers grew more severe in textiles and deformable bodies. While Isaac Sim and Newton performed well in slow, quasi-static textile pulling, Isaac Sim's normalized RMSE exploded to 128.26 during dynamic textile flinging, compared to 8.54 for Genesis. In 3D deformable tasks, Genesis led in pulling and twisting, but all engines exhibited errors roughly 10 times the empirical baseline variance.

5.2 World Model Results: Right Equations, Wrong Numbers
Most video models generated visually plausible constant-acceleration and pendulum motions. Yet, despite high equation fit metrics ($R^2$ and QFI), the derived physical parameters diverged dramatically from reality. In free fall, for instance, Cosmos3-Super-I2V produced trajectories fitting a parabola closely (a strong QFI of 12.50), but its estimated gravitational acceleration was just $0.088\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Even the closest model, Seedance 2, reached only $1.84\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, far below Earth's gravity of roughly $9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

In the pendulum task, Wan-2.2 and Genie 3 exhibited near-perfect periodic motion with $R^2 = 0.99$, yet their periods hovered around 1.9 seconds—roughly 73% to 80% slower than the real-world period of 1.06 seconds. Furthermore, adding negative prompts produced inconsistent effects across tasks and models, showing that robust physical laws are not yet embedded.

captions.F4: Fitting results for physical trajectories extracted from generated videos. In the pendulum task (c), models show varying trajectory damping directions and periods; even with a near-perfect R^2 of 0.99, models oscillate at periods more than 70% slower than the real-world period (1.06 s).

sections.heading: Extending to fluids and 3D world model evaluations
sections.summary: Current limitations of GAUGE include a restricted range of materials and physical parameters, as well as the absence of fluids and coupled interactions. Furthermore, world model evaluations are currently limited to 2D rigid trajectories, motivating future extensions to 3D point clouds and meshes for deformable objects.
sections.details:
The authors highlight two primary directions for future work.

First, expanding material and physical phenomenon coverage. While GAUGE covers rigid bodies, textiles, and deformable solids, real-world material properties shift significantly with surface finishing, temperature, manufacturing batches, and wear. Future work needs to span wider ranges of friction coefficients, stiffness, and damping ratios. Additionally, incorporating fluids such as water and oil, along with coupled fluid-structure interaction (FSI) simulations with rigid and soft bodies, is essential for robots interacting with real environments.

Second, expanding the dimensionality of world model evaluation. Currently, video generation model evaluation is restricted to 2D tracking of rigid bodies with minimal depth change. However, textile and soft-body behaviors feature complex 3D phenomena like self-occlusion, wrinkling, and twisting that cannot be captured by tracking a 2D center of mass. In the future, directly reconstructing 3D point clouds or surface meshes from generated videos will enable evaluations based on local strain, volume change, curvature, and geodesic distortion. A key challenge will be formulating models that cleanly disentangle 3D reconstruction perceptual errors from the world model's underlying physical errors.

sections.heading: Diagnosing physical fidelity to advance embodied AI
sections.summary: By grounding evaluation in real-world measurements and physical properties, GAUGE enables unified diagnostics of physical fidelity across simulators and world models. Moving beyond visual quality and isolated metrics to assess both governing equations and parameter scales forms the cornerstone for next-generation embodied AI.
sections.details:
This paper presented GAUGE, a benchmark designed to evaluate the physical fidelity of numerical physics engines and generative video world models grounded in real-world measurements. Combining 22 standardized task families, high-precision motion-capture trajectories, and experimentally identified physical parameters, it provides a rigorous diagnostic platform that moves past appearance-based evaluation.

The findings are clear: leading physics engines exhibit specialized strengths and face major hurdles in impulsive collisions, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation. Meanwhile, generative video world models can produce smooth, equation-like trajectories while dramatically misjudging basic physical scales like acceleration and oscillation periods.

Relying solely on visual realism or simple trajectory distance metrics cannot yield truly reliable simulators or world models. By evaluating equation structures, physical parameters, and temporal dynamics against ground-truth measurements, the GAUGE framework marks an important step forward for simulation technologies in embodied AI.

sections.heading: Detailed physical measurement methods and contact geometry variations
sections.summary: The appendix details measurement techniques for friction and restitution coefficients using an inclined track and air-bearing rails, Poisson's ratio measurement via DIC, and anisotropic stiffness mapping for fabrics. It also outlines the geometric variations of wedges and pyramids used in nonsmooth contact tasks.
sections.details:
The appendix provides detailed procedures for the material property calibrations introduced in the main text.

- Measuring Friction and Restitution Coefficients:
Friction coefficients between rigid bodies, and between rigid bodies and textiles, were identified by sliding objects on a precision inclined track and back-calculating from acceleration. To isolate restitution from friction, objects were collided on an inclined air-bearing rail, computing the pure coefficient of restitution $e$ from velocity ratios before and after impact.

- Textile and Deformable Material Characterization:
Textile tensile, shear, and bending stiffness were measured along warp, weft, and bias directions using a Style3D measurement system. For simulation setups, these values were mapped to effective isotropic stiffnesses matching each engine's constitutive model. For deformable bodies, Young's moduli were derived from initial linear regions of stress-strain curves on a compression testing machine, while concurrent DIC analysis calculated Poisson's ratios from the ratio of transverse expansion to longitudinal strain.

- Geometric Variations in Nonsmooth Contact Tasks:
To go beyond simple planar impacts, three geometric pairings were designed: square pyramid with square groove, square pyramid with triangular groove, and wedge with triangular groove. These test how well engines reproduce discontinuous contact dynamics caused by interlocking surfaces.

takeaways: Do not be fooled by world model visual quality: even when models generate smooth periodic or falling motions, their internal accelerations and periods often differ from the real world by more than a factor of two.

No physics engine is universally superior: Isaac Sim excels in steady rigid-body contact, Genesis in rapid textile motion and deformable bodies, and Newton in specific bending behaviors, making engine selection task-dependent.

Impulsive contact and high-speed deformation remain major Sim2Real bottlenecks: instantaneous momentum transfer (like Newton's cradle) and dynamic cloth flinging remain exceptionally challenging for current simulators.

Physics evaluation requires separating equation structure from parameter accuracy: beyond high $R^2$ values, models must be diagnosed individually on whether their gravitational accelerations and damping coefficients match physical constants.
limitations: World model evaluations are currently limited to 2D rigid-body trajectories, without directly evaluating complex 3D deformation, self-contact, or depth changes in textiles and soft bodies.
Material behavior varies with environmental conditions (temperature, humidity, wear), but the covered material types and physical parameter ranges remain limited.
Fluids such as water and oil, as well as coupled fluid-structure interactions (FSI), are not included in the task suite.
